posts.topic: the 3 things event organizers read first in a speaker pitch
posts.hook: Event organizers scan your pitch in 12 seconds
posts.body:
Here's what they read first:

1. Your core message in one sentence
Not your bio. Not your credentials. What specific problem do you solve?

2. Your audience impact statement
How many people will walk away changed? What transformation happens?

3. Your recent speaking experience
They want proof you can deliver. List your last 3 events with audience sizes.

4. Your availability window
Don't make them guess. Give specific dates you can speak.

5. Your fee structure upfront
Hiding your rates wastes everyone's time. Be transparent.

The speakers who get booked nail these five things before organizers even scroll down.

Stop burying the important stuff in paragraph three.

— Reeve

posts.topic: why most speakers only get booked once at the same event
posts.hook: Most speakers think getting booked once means they've 'made it' with that client.
posts.body:
Most speakers think getting booked once means they've 'made it' with that client.

Then they disappear.

No follow-up. No check-ins. No value between events.

They treat each gig like a one-night stand instead of the beginning of a relationship.

Meanwhile, the speakers who get invited back year after year do these things differently:

They stay in touch with event planners between bookings.

They share relevant content and insights throughout the year.

They ask about next year's event before this year's is even over.

They understand that speaking isn't about transactions.

It's about relationships.

One great talk opens the door. Consistent follow-up keeps it open.

Your best clients aren't the ones you haven't met yet. They're sitting in your past client list.

— Reeve

posts.topic: unpaid speaking gigs — when they're worth it and when they're not
posts.hook: Most speakers say yes to every unpaid gig. Big mistake.
posts.body:
Free speaking isn't always free money lost.

Say yes when:
• The audience matches your ideal client profile exactly
• You can test new material before paying gigs
• The event organizer has serious influence in your industry
• You get video content that showcases your best stories
• The networking potential is worth more than your fee

Say no when:
• They expect you to pay for travel
• The audience has zero buying power
• No video recording allowed
• You're filling a last-minute cancellation
• They won't provide attendee contact information

Your time has value. Make sure every unpaid gig pays you back somehow.

— Reeve

posts.topic: what separates speakers who get callbacks from those who don't
posts.hook: The speakers who get callbacks never wait for permission to follow up.
posts.body:
Most speakers think their job ends when they walk off stage.

The ones who get rebooked? They're already planning their next conversation with the event planner.

They send thank you notes within 24 hours. Not generic ones — specific mentions of audience reactions or questions that came up.

They share photos and video clips from their talk. They tag the organization and highlight key moments.

They ask for feedback. Not just "how did I do?" but "what would make this even better for your audience next year?"

They stay connected. LinkedIn requests to attendees. Comments on the organization's posts. Genuine relationship building.

While other speakers hope their performance was enough, callback speakers are actively nurturing the relationship.

Your talk opens the door. Your follow-up keeps it open.

— Reeve

posts.topic: the speaker pipeline problem nobody talks about
posts.hook: Most speakers have a pipeline problem they don't even know exists
posts.body:
You're focusing on the wrong metrics.

1. You count rejections instead of tracking follow-ups

2. You measure event size instead of audience quality

3. You chase fee increases instead of building relationships

4. You book one-offs instead of creating repeat clients

5. You wait for referrals instead of nurturing your network

The best speakers know their pipeline isn't about volume.
It's about relationships that compound over time.

Start treating speaking like a relationship business, not a transactional one.

— Reeve

posts.topic: why your speaker bio is losing you bookings
posts.hook: Your bio reads like everyone else's — and that's why you're not getting booked
posts.body:
Event planners scan hundreds of bios every week.

Most sound identical: "Dynamic speaker who transforms audiences through powerful insights."

Boring. Generic. Forgettable.

Here's what actually gets you noticed:

Specific outcomes you deliver. Not "I inspire people" but "I help teams reduce conflict by 40% in 90 days."

Your unique angle on mindset work. What makes your approach different from the 500 other mindset speakers?

Client results that matter. Numbers, stories, measurable change.

Personality that shows through the words. Let them feel who you are, not just what you do.

A clear promise for their audience. What will people walk away thinking, feeling, or doing?

Your bio isn't a resume. It's a preview of the experience you create.

Make it impossible to ignore.

— Reeve

posts.topic: how systematic pitching is changing who gets booked to speak in 2026
posts.hook: Event planners stopped waiting for perfect speakers to appear.
posts.body:
Event planners stopped waiting for perfect speakers to appear.

They're booking speakers who show up consistently in their inbox with relevant topics.

The old model was reactive. Wait for referrals. Wait for inbound requests. Wait to be discovered.

The new model is systematic. Research events. Craft targeted pitches. Follow up strategically.

Speakers who built systematic outreach processes are getting 3-5x more bookings than those waiting to be invited.

They track which events book their topics. They know decision maker names. They pitch 90 days before planning cycles.

Meanwhile, talented speakers with no system watch opportunities go to speakers who simply showed up first.

Your expertise matters. But your process determines who sees it.

— Reeve

posts.topic: the follow-up rule most speakers ignore after they speak
posts.hook: You just delivered an incredible keynote. Then you disappear.
posts.body:
The biggest mistake speakers make happens after they leave the stage.

They pack up. They fly home. They wait for the next invitation.

Meanwhile, the event organizer is already planning next year's lineup. Your audience is buzzing about what they learned. The networking opportunities are still warm.

But you're gone.

Smart speakers know the real work starts when the applause ends. They follow up within 48 hours. They connect with attendees on LinkedIn. They send thank-you notes to organizers.

Most importantly, they ask for referrals while the experience is fresh.

The speakers who book consistently aren't the ones who give the best talks. They're the ones who turn every speaking opportunity into three more.

Your next gig isn't waiting in your inbox. It's hiding in your last event's aftermath.

— Reeve

posts.topic: building a speaking pipeline: what it actually looks like
posts.hook: Most speakers think a pipeline means waiting for event planners to call
posts.body:
Here's what building a speaking pipeline actually looks like:

1. Research 50 events in your industry every month

2. Send 3 pitches per week to decision makers

3. Follow up twice after initial outreach

4. Track every conversation in a simple spreadsheet

5. Book discovery calls, not just speaking gigs

The speakers who get consistent bookings treat it like sales.

They don't wait to be discovered.

They create their own opportunities through systematic outreach.

Your expertise means nothing if nobody knows about it.

— Reeve

posts.topic: client result — first booking in the pipeline
posts.hook: We submitted 5 pitches. One said yes. The speaker made $4,500.
posts.body:
Week one: we scanned 40 open conferences in the speaker's niche.

We found five that were actively looking for their exact topic. All five had open CFP windows.

Five targeted pitches went out in 48 hours. We wrote them. We sent them.

By day 14: one acceptance. A regional leadership summit. 300 attendees. $4,500 keynote fee plus travel.

The speaker found out via email from us.

They didn't have to research the conference, write the pitch, or manage the follow-up.

They just showed up and spoke.

That's what a pipeline looks like when it's actually running.

posts.topic: client result — what 90 days of consistent pitching looks like
posts.hook: Month 1 with Reeve: 8 pitches sent. Month 3: first paid keynote booked.
posts.body:
The first month is slow.

We're building the pipeline, learning which conferences match the speaker's niche, and writing the first round of pitches. Nothing comes back yes yet.

Month two: follow-ups go out. Three conferences ask for more information. One wants a call.

Month three: the call becomes a booking. A corporate summit. 400 attendees. $6,000 fee.

This isn't magic. It's math.

Most speakers quit before month three because they don't have a system that keeps pitching when they're busy preparing for other talks.

Consistency is the product. The booking is the proof.

— Reeve

posts.topic: how to set your speaking fee — a practical framework
posts.hook: Most speakers underprice by $2,000 because they guess
posts.body:
Here's the fee-setting framework that actually works:

1. Anchor to audience size
Under 100 people = $1,500–$3,000
100–500 people = $3,000–$7,500
500+ people = $7,500–$15,000+
Thousands = your number

2. Add premium for industry
Corporate pays 2–3x what nonprofits pay.
Tech, finance, and healthcare pay most.
Associations and education pay least.

3. Factor in exclusivity
Will you compete with yourself nearby? Add a geographic exclusivity surcharge.

4. Build in a travel buffer
Never include flights in your quote — invoice separately.

5. Set a floor and hold it
Discount once and it becomes your new price forever.

Your fee isn't what you're worth.
It's what the market will bear when you're positioned correctly.

Position first. Then set your number.

— Reeve

posts.topic: what your one-sheet is actually for
posts.hook: Your one-sheet isn't for you to feel professional. It's a buying decision tool.
posts.body:
Event planners don't read one-sheets to learn about you.

They read them to answer one question: will my audience respond to this person?

Every element needs to answer that question:

Your headshot should show confidence and approachability. Not a corporate mugshot. Not a casual selfie.

Your topic title should promise a specific outcome. "Leadership Excellence" means nothing. "How to Keep Your Best People From Leaving" means everything.

Your bio should focus on results, not resume. Where you've spoken is table stakes. What changed in the room is the pitch.

Your testimonials need specifics. "Best speaker we've ever had" is noise. "Our engagement scores went up 28% that quarter" is signal.

Your contact information must be immediate and obvious.

Every line on that page should make the decision easier.

If it doesn't help them say yes, cut it.

— Reeve

posts.topic: niche clarity — why narrowing down gets you more stages
posts.hook: The speakers who try to appeal to everyone book the least stages.
posts.body:
It feels counterintuitive.

Surely a broader message means more opportunity.

But event planners aren't booking "inspiring speakers."

They're booking the person who speaks specifically to nurses dealing with burnout. Or CFOs navigating private equity transitions. Or founders preparing for their first fundraise.

Specificity is credibility.

When you try to speak to everyone, you signal to event planners that you haven't done the work to know your real audience.

The speakers who book consistently have one clear answer to: "Who specifically is this for?"

That answer makes their pitch easier to place. It makes their marketing easier to write. It makes their audience experience better.

Your niche isn't a limitation. It's the thing that makes you the obvious choice for a specific room.

Stop trying to be right for everyone. Start being undeniably right for someone.

— Reeve

posts.topic: imposter syndrome before a big stage — what actually helps
posts.hook: The night before a $10,000 keynote, most speakers feel like a fraud.
posts.body:
Not because they are one.

Because their brain is trying to protect them from potential embarrassment.

Here's what doesn't help: telling yourself you're good enough. Positive affirmations in the mirror. Pretending the nerves aren't there.

Here's what does:

Review your evidence file. Every piece of positive feedback you've ever received. Every outcome you've driven. Every person who said you changed the way they think.

Get into your opening. The first 90 seconds are your anchor. If you know those cold, your nervous system settles.

Remember who you're there for. The energy shifts when you stop thinking about being evaluated and start thinking about the person in row four who needed to hear what you're about to say.

The nerves don't mean you're not ready. They mean you care.

That caring is what makes the talk land.

— Reeve

posts.topic: the minimal CRM setup that keeps a speaking pipeline moving
posts.hook: You don't need expensive software to run a speaking pipeline.
posts.body:
Speakers overcomplicate this.

You need to track five things per conference contact:
1. Name and organization
2. Date you pitched
3. Date you followed up
4. Their response (yes / no / no response / not yet)
5. Their planning cycle — when do they book for next year?

That's it. A spreadsheet does this. A basic Notion table does this.

What matters isn't the tool. It's the discipline.

Every Friday: 15 minutes to update status, schedule next follow-ups, and note any responses that came in that week.

Speakers who do this weekly never lose a warm lead. Speakers who skip it spend months chasing conversations they should have closed.

Your pipeline isn't a lead tracking problem. It's a consistency problem.

Pick any tool. Work it every week. Watch what happens.

— Reeve

posts.topic: two hours per week to a full speaking pipeline — the schedule
posts.hook: A full speaking pipeline fits in two hours a week
posts.body:
Here's the weekly schedule that keeps the pipeline moving:

Monday — 30 minutes
Research 5–8 new conferences in your niche.
Check application deadlines. Find decision-maker names.

Tuesday — 20 minutes
Write and send 2 new pitches.
Use a template. Personalize the first paragraph only.

Wednesday — 10 minutes
Follow up on any pitch sent 10–14 days ago with no response.
One sentence. Polite. Direct.

Friday — 15 minutes
Update your tracker.
Log any responses. Schedule next follow-ups.

Total: ~75 minutes

The speakers building real pipelines aren't doing more.
They're doing this consistently.

Two hours a week, every week, for 6 months.
That's how the pipeline fills.

— Reeve

posts.topic: kill fees — what they are and why you need them in every contract
posts.hook: You got booked. Then they cancelled. You got paid nothing.
posts.body:
This happens more than speakers admit.

Event gets cancelled. Organizer says sorry. Your calendar had that date blocked for three months. You turned down other gigs.

Without a kill fee clause, you have no recourse.

A kill fee is a cancellation penalty that protects your time:

60+ days out: 25–50% of your fee
30–59 days out: 50–75% of your fee
Under 30 days: 100% of your fee

Incorporate this into your speaker agreement before it becomes a problem.

Most event organizers won't fight it — this is industry standard. The ones who push back are showing you something important about how they operate.

You built something valuable enough for them to book. That value doesn't disappear when their plans change.

Protect your calendar like the asset it is.

— Reeve

posts.topic: the fee ladder — how to move clients from free to full rate
posts.hook: Most speakers either charge full rate or speak free. The fee ladder is the move in between.
posts.body:
The fee ladder is how you turn relationships into bookings without leaving money on the table.

Here's how it works:

You start with a reduced rate for a client who's new, small-budget, or a strategic fit. You set a clear expectation: this rate is for now.

You deliver an excellent talk. You get the testimonial, the video, the referrals.

Next time they book: your rate reflects what you know you're worth.

Three rules make this work:

1. Put the reduced rate in writing — including what the standard rate will be next year.

2. Never reduce your stated rate. Offer add-ons, extras, or value instead.

3. Treat every discounted talk like a paid sponsorship. You're investing in that relationship, not apologizing for your price.

Moving up the fee ladder requires you to have one. Build it on purpose.

— Reeve

posts.topic: how to read a CFP — what they're actually asking for
posts.hook: Most speakers skim CFPs. Then wonder why they don't get selected.
posts.body:
Here's what conference selection committees are actually looking for:

1. Fit with the theme
Every CFP has a stated theme. Mirror that language back. Show you read it.

2. Audience level match
Is this a beginner track or advanced? Pitch accordingly.

3. Evidence of delivery
They're not buying your idea. They're buying your ability to execute it in a room.

4. Specific takeaways
List 3 things attendees will leave knowing or able to do. Be concrete.

5. Speaker credibility signal
One sentence of relevant proof. A past talk to a similar audience. A measurable outcome.

6. No jargon
Write your abstract in plain English. Every sentence should be clear to someone who doesn't know your field.

The CFP isn't a form. It's a preview of how you communicate.

Write it like the room is already full.

— Reeve

posts.topic: your opening 90 seconds — why everything depends on them
posts.hook: Audiences decide in the first 90 seconds whether they're with you.
posts.body:
Not whether your talk is worth attending.

Whether you're worth listening to.

That decision happens before you've made your first point. Before you've told your biggest story. Before you've earned the laugh.

The speakers who command rooms know this.

Their opening is engineered. Not memorized — engineered. The first line creates a pattern interrupt. The second creates a question they need answered. The third establishes who they are without listing their credentials.

Most speakers waste their first 90 seconds on logistics, thank-yous, and warm-up jokes that don't land.

Start in the middle of something. Start with a number that doesn't make sense. Start with the question that woke you up at 3am.

Start where you want their attention to be — not where you feel comfortable beginning.

Your opening is not the setup. It's the talk.

— Reeve

posts.topic: conference calendar mapping — how to know which events to pitch 6 months out
posts.hook: Event planners lock in speakers 6–9 months before the event. Most speakers pitch too late.
posts.body:
The application window closes long before you hear about the event.

By the time a conference is promoted publicly, the speaker roster is already set.

Speakers who book consistently work the other direction: they build a conference calendar and work backwards from event dates.

How:

1. Search your niche + "2026 conference" or "annual summit."

2. Find last year's dates. This year's dates are usually within two weeks of the same.

3. Find the CFP from last year. Note when it opened and closed.

4. Add a calendar reminder 6 months before this year's projected event date.

Repeat for 20–30 events in your niche.

Now you have an outreach calendar instead of a reactive inbox.

The best stages don't wait for you to notice them. You have to already be watching.

— Reeve

posts.topic: how to use a rejection as a pitch sharpener
posts.hook: Getting a "no" from a conference is the most useful data you'll get all month.
posts.body:
Not if you ignore it.

Most speakers file rejections under "not a fit" and move on. The ones who book consistently treat them differently.

They reply to declines with a single question: "Can you tell me what the talk was missing?"

Fifty percent of the time, they get an answer.

That answer is worth more than the rejection cost.

"Your topic was covered last year" → update your CFP angle and pitch again in two years.

"We needed more case studies" → build a results page before next round of pitches.

"Great submission, but we overfilled that track" → ask to be added to the waitlist, follow up in spring.

The speakers who improve fastest aren't the ones with the most talent. They're the ones who collect the most feedback.

Turn every no into a question. Let the answers rewrite your pitch.

— Reeve

posts.topic: the batch research day that fills your conference pipeline
posts.hook: Two hours on a Sunday. That's all it takes to fill a 90-day conference pipeline.
posts.body:
Here's the batch:

Hour 1 — Discovery
Search "[your niche] conference 2026" + "[your niche] summit 2026."
Open every result in a new tab. Skip any with no speaker application link.
You should find 20–30 possibilities.

Hour 2 — Triage
For each one: Is the audience my buyer? Does the topic fit my talk? Is the CFP open?
If yes to all three → add to pipeline. If not → close the tab.

You'll end the session with 8–12 qualified targets, each with a deadline and a decision-maker name.

That's your next 90 days.

Do this every month and the pipeline never runs dry.

Do it never and you spend all year reacting to opportunities that are already closed.

— Reeve

posts.topic: speaker agreement essentials — 5 clauses you cannot skip
posts.hook: Most speaker agreements are missing the clauses that actually protect you
posts.body:
Here are the 5 clauses every speaker agreement needs:

1. Kill fee
60+ days out = 50%. Under 30 days = 100%.
Your calendar is inventory. Cancelled bookings need to cost the organizer.

2. Recording rights
Who owns the video? Can they post it without credit? Define this upfront.
Ideal: organizer keeps internal rights, you get full rights after 12 months.

3. Travel reimbursement cap
Set a maximum. Require pre-approval for anything over $300.
Unlimited travel commitments become liability.

4. Postponement clause
Distinct from cancellation. If they postpone > 60 days, treat as a new booking with revised terms.

5. Topic exclusivity window
If they want you not to speak on this topic at a competing event, they pay an exclusivity surcharge.

None of these are aggressive.
All of them are standard.
And none of them protect you unless they're in writing.

— Reeve

posts.topic: speaker showcases — how to get on the radar of event planners fast
posts.hook: The fastest way to get booked isn't a cold pitch. It's a live audience of event planners.
posts.body:
Speaker showcases exist for exactly this reason.

NSA (National Speakers Association) chapters run them monthly. So do PCMA, MPI, and most regional speaker bureaus.

Format: 10–15 minutes on stage in front of 30–50 meeting planners, event directors, and bureau agents.

Cost: usually free or under $100 for non-members.

What you get: real-time feedback, instant referrals, and your name in a room full of people who book speakers for a living.

Most speakers skip showcases because they don't know they exist or think they're not ready.

They're wrong on both counts.

You find them by searching your niche + "speaker showcase" + your city or region.

Or by joining your local NSA chapter and showing up.

The speakers in the room who get booked fastest aren't always the best. They're the most visible.

Get in the room.

— Reeve

posts.topic: talking about your fee without apologizing for it
posts.hook: The moment you apologize for your fee, you've already lost the negotiation.
posts.body:
It happens in the pause before you say the number.

The slight drop in your voice. The qualifier. "We can talk about what works for your budget."

That's not flexibility. That's a signal that you don't believe your price.

Event planners are trained to spot it.

Here's what confident fee communication sounds like:

"My fee for a 45-minute keynote is $7,500 plus travel. That includes prep calls and a post-event Q&A if needed."

Full stop. No apology. No qualifier. No offer to discount before they've even asked.

If they push back: "That's our standard rate. What's your budget?"

Then you listen. Then you decide whether the fit is worth a conversation.

But you name your number first, clearly, and let it stand.

Speakers who earn top fees aren't necessarily better. They're clearer about what they charge and why.

— Reeve

posts.topic: tracking your pitch acceptance rate — and what good looks like
posts.hook: Most speakers have no idea what their pitch acceptance rate is. That's the real problem.
posts.body:
If you don't track it, you can't improve it.

Here's what good looks like:

Cold pitches to conferences with open CFPs: 5–15% acceptance is normal.
Targeted pitches to conferences where your topic is a close match: 20–35% is achievable.
Warm pitches (referral or prior relationship): 40–60% with the right follow-up.

If your rate is below 5%, the problem is almost never your topic. It's one of these:
— Pitching too broad ("leadership" to a niche tech conference)
— Missing the CFP window (apply 3–6 months before the event)
— No evidence of delivery (conference websites, testimonials, video)

If you don't know your rate, start tracking now. Even a basic spreadsheet: pitched, response, accepted/declined.

Three months of data shows you where your funnel is leaking.

The speakers who book consistently aren't luckier. They're the ones who looked at their numbers.

— Reeve

posts.topic: the follow-up sequence that doesn't feel like nagging
posts.hook: Most speakers either never follow up or follow up too much. Here's the sequence that works.
posts.body:
After your initial pitch, follow this sequence:

Day 0: Send your pitch.
Personalized subject. One-sheet attached. Clear ask.

Day 14: First follow-up.
2 sentences. Reference your original. One direct question: "Is this on your radar?"

Day 30: Second follow-up.
1 sentence. "Wanted to make sure this didn't get buried."
If no response after this — move them to a 90-day bucket.

Day 90: Third and final.
"I know timing matters for programming — circling back in case fall planning is starting."

That's it. Three touches over 90 days.

The rule: never apologize. Never pressure. Always make it easy to say yes.

After touch 3 with no response: mark the conference as "low priority" and focus energy on warmer prospects.

Consistency > volume.
A 3-touch sequence on 10 conferences beats a single pitch to 50.

— Reeve

posts.topic: saying no to misfit gigs — why it protects your reputation
posts.hook: Every gig you take that isn't right for your audience makes the next booking harder.
posts.body:
Speaking to the wrong room isn't neutral.

It's an active cost.

When you speak to an audience that isn't your buyer — wrong industry, wrong seniority, wrong context — you produce content and testimonials that don't match your positioning.

Then you show that video to your next target audience. The mismatch is obvious.

The event planner who was almost a yes becomes a no.

The speakers who build the most valuable pipelines are selective early. Not because of ego — because of positioning.

Every stage you take leaves a trace: the conference brand, the audience type, the industry context. That trace either reinforces your positioning or dilutes it.

A $4,000 talk at the wrong conference isn't $4,000 earned. It's positioning capital spent.

Be honest about which rooms you belong in. Then only say yes to those.

— Reeve

posts.topic: speaker agreement vs verbal confirmation — why speakers keep getting burned
posts.hook: "We'd love to have you" is not a booking. It's a conversation starter.
posts.body:
Speakers lose gigs they thought were confirmed because they never got anything in writing.

Here's the timeline that trips them up:

Event planner says yes on a call. Speaker blocks the date. Speaker turns down another opportunity. Two months later: "We went in a different direction."

No contract means no kill fee. No kill fee means no recovery.

Here's the fix: make it a policy and say it out loud.

"I'll hold the date for 48 hours — as soon as I get a signed agreement, it's locked in."

Most planners respond well to this. It signals professionalism. It tells them you take your commitments seriously.

The ones who push back on signing anything are showing you something important.

Your time has value. Paper protects it.

Don't block your calendar for a verbal.

— Reeve

posts.topic: the ROI question organizers think but never ask
posts.hook: Event planners are always calculating your ROI. Most speakers never help them.
posts.body:
Every booking decision has a business case behind it.

The event planner doesn't just want a great speaker. They need to justify the spend to their director, their board, or their conference committee.

Your pitch almost never addresses this.

Here's what they're actually calculating:
- Will this speaker's topic drive attendance?
- Will this talk produce shareable content that justifies our investment?
- Can I use this booking to attract a sponsor?
- Is this speaker's name recognizable enough to put on the website?

The speakers who make this easy get booked more.

How: in your pitch, add one line that does the ROI work for them.

"My topic consistently trends on LinkedIn after events — past talks have driven 200+ post-event shares."

"I'm happy to co-promote the event to my 12,000 followers once I'm confirmed."

Give them the business case. Close the mental tab they're trying to fill.

— Reeve
